vignette:
Omar Haddad was 34 when he came to treatment, a married man working as a publisher in a busy office where much of his day was spent moving between editorial meetings, author lunches, print deadlines, and the public-facing routines of the literary world. The event he returned to again and again involved his wife, and even when he tried to describe it in sequence, it came out in pieces. He would begin with the bus, then a sound, then the shock of seeing her exposed and helpless, then a gap. What remained most vividly were disconnected fragments and the sense that the whole thing had never settled into a single story in his mind.

Months earlier, Omar and his wife had been riding a city bus home in the evening. He remembered the crowded aisle, the stale heat, the tiredness that had settled into him after a long workday, and then the abrupt eruption of fear when an incident on the bus left his wife injured and vulnerable in public. In his recollection, the images did not arrive as a smooth narrative. Instead there was the flash of her body partially uncovered, the humiliation of strangers staring, the metallic rattle of the bus, someone shouting, and the sound of her voice that he still heard in his head at unwanted moments. Sometimes what returned to him was not even a picture at first but the auditory trace of that scene—the screech of brakes, raised voices, his wife crying out. At other times the memory ran like a film that started without warning and replayed with the same merciless clarity, as if he were back there watching the worst seconds repeat.

In the weeks that followed, Omar found that ordinary parts of life had become charged in ways he could not control. Riding a bus was out of the question. Even seeing one pull up at a stop on his commute made his body tense, his mind already filling in what could happen in the enclosed space among strangers. He began arranging rides, paying for car services, or walking long distances rather than using public transport. This affected his work quickly. Publishing had once required flexibility—traveling across the city to meet booksellers, attending events in unfamiliar venues, visiting printers and partner offices—but Omar started declining assignments that required him to cross town if he did not know exactly what the place looked like and how he would get there. He was certain that unfamiliar places put him at a disadvantage because he could not immediately judge where danger might come from, what objects could be used as weapons, or whether the people around him were safe.

That way of scanning had become nearly constant. In conference rooms, cafés, lobbies, and even at small literary receptions, his attention went first to faces and hands. He studied expressions, posture, tone, any flicker that might signal threat. He noticed letter openers on desks, heavy glass bottles, metal staplers, kitchen knives at catered events—objects other people ignored but that, to Omar, stood out with alarming immediacy. His colleagues experienced him as distracted or overly serious; his wife saw how little rest he got even when they were at home. He told her he could not stop checking people. He needed to know who might turn dangerous.

His sense of vulnerability had also narrowed around his own body. Being undressed, especially stepping out of the shower or changing clothes, brought a sharp and disproportionate unease. In those moments he felt exposed in a way that immediately called up his wife’s public vulnerability on the bus, and he hurried through dressing, avoiding lingering in that state even in the privacy of home. Exhaustion made everything worse in his day-to-day experience. If he was very tired after late-night manuscript deadlines or a long book fair, the memories came more easily and felt less containable. On those days the replay in his mind seemed closer to the surface, and the sounds from the event intruded more forcefully.

By the time he sought help, these habits had accumulated into a smaller life. He was still working, but with increasing strain. He had begun passing opportunities to travel for the press and avoiding new venues unless someone else could go first and tell him what to expect. At home, his wife had noticed how often he startled into vigilance in ordinary settings and how rigidly he organized routes and routines. Omar came to treatment after a work obligation forced him onto a bus substitute during a transit disruption, and the combination of the crowded vehicle, end-of-day exhaustion, and the sight of strangers’ faces around him left him shaken for hours. What frightened him most was not only the return of the memory, in fragments and sound and replay, but the conviction that he was no longer able to move through the world without constantly preparing for danger. What he hoped for, quietly but urgently, was to be able to accompany his wife through ordinary life again without feeling that exposure and threat were waiting in every crowd.
